title: Chapter 7 Drill: Liver, Biliary Tract, Pancreas, and Spleen

items.stem: A 61-year-old man has painless jaundice and a pancreatic head mass. Serum immunoglobulin G4 is markedly elevated. Computed tomography shows a diffusely enlarged pancreas with a capsule-like rim and a long smooth biliary stricture. Which treatment should be started first?
items.explanation: A diffusely enlarged featureless gland, elevated immunoglobulin G4, and a long smooth stricture suggest autoimmune pancreatitis, an immune-mediated disorder that responds to corticosteroids, often within weeks. Confirming the diagnosis is important because resection for presumed cancer is unnecessary in these patients. Chemotherapy has no role, and stenting alone does not address the inflammation causing the stricture.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man with cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis B vomits a large volume of bright red blood. Heart rate is 124 and blood pressure 88/50 mm Hg. He is given restrictive transfusion, and an intravenous vasoactive infusion is started. Which additional measures are most appropriate before and during endoscopy?
options: Balloon tamponade tube as first-line therapy
Prophylactic antibiotic and endoscopic band ligation of the varices
Intravenous proton pump infusion as the only added therapy
items.explanation: Acute variceal hemorrhage is managed with a vasoactive agent such as octreotide, short-course antibiotic prophylaxis, which lowers infection and mortality, and endoscopic band ligation within 12 hours. Balloon tamponade is a bridge for failed endoscopic control. Emergency surgical shunting carries high mortality and is a rescue option. Acid suppression alone does not treat variceal bleeding, and it is not a substitute for these measures.

items.stem: A 5-year-old girl has recurrent episodes of abdominal pain and mild jaundice. Imaging shows fusiform dilation of the extrahepatic bile duct to 2.5 cm without intrahepatic involvement. Which management is most appropriate?
items.explanation: A fusiform extrahepatic dilation is a type I choledochal cyst, which carries a lifelong risk of cholangiocarcinoma, stones, and cholangitis. The standard operation is complete excision of the cyst, including the gallbladder, with Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy. Drainage procedures leave the diseased epithelium in place, so malignancy risk persists. Stent surveillance and delay only prolong exposure to complications.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man is in week four of necrotizing gallstone pancreatitis. He has new fever and leukocytosis. Computed tomography shows a walled-off collection of 12 cm with gas bubbles within the necrosis. He is hemodynamically stable. Which approach is best?
options: Antibiotics alone with no drainage because he is stable
items.explanation: Gas within walled-off necrosis with sepsis indicates infected necrosis. Delay to about four weeks lets the necrosis wall off, and a step-up strategy, starting with antibiotics and endoscopic or percutaneous drainage and escalating to minimally invasive necrosectomy, lowers major complications and death compared with primary open necrosectomy. Antibiotics alone rarely clear a large infected collection, and total pancreatectomy is not indicated.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman has jaundice and a 3 cm pancreatic head adenocarcinoma. Computed tomography shows tumor contact with the superior mesenteric vein of more than 180 degrees without arterial involvement and no distant metastases. How is this tumor best classified and managed?
options: Borderline resectable, with neoadjuvant chemotherapy before attempted resection
Locally advanced, with surgical bypass as definitive treatment
items.explanation: Venous contact beyond 180 degrees without arterial encasement defines borderline resectable disease. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy improves the chance of a margin-negative resection and selects patients with favorable tumor biology before major surgery. Immediate resection risks a positive margin and early recurrence. Unresectability implies arterial encasement or metastases, and bypass alone offers no cure for a potentially operable tumor.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has episodic postprandial right upper quadrant pain for eight months with nausea. Ultrasound, upper endoscopy, and liver tests are normal. A cholecystokinin-stimulated nuclear scan shows a gallbladder ejection fraction of 22 percent, and the infusion reproduces her pain. Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: Endoscopic sphincterotomy of the biliary sphincter
Repeat scan in one year before any intervention
items.explanation: Typical biliary pain with a normal ultrasound and an abnormally low ejection fraction, with symptom reproduction on stimulation, is biliary dyskinesia, an acalculous gallbladder disorder. Cholecystectomy relieves symptoms in most carefully selected patients. Acid suppression does not address a functional gallbladder problem, and sphincterotomy is for sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, not this. Waiting prolongs disability without improving the diagnosis.

items.stem: On day nine after a pancreaticoduodenectomy complicated by a leak, a patient has a small amount of bright red blood in the drain, followed hours later by a large gastrointestinal bleed with hypotension. Which source is most likely, and what is the best initial management of a stabilized patient?
options: Gastroduodenal artery stump pseudoaneurysm treated by angiographic embolization
Stress ulcer treated with endoscopic banding
Portal vein thrombosis treated by thrombolysis
Anastomotic suture line bleed treated by immediate observation
items.explanation: A herald bleed in a drain after a pancreatic leak suggests an arterial pseudoaneurysm, typically at the gastroduodenal artery stump, caused by enzyme erosion. A stable patient is best managed with angiography and embolization or covered stent, with reoperation if unstable or angiography fails. Stress ulcers do not usually present with drain blood, and portal thrombosis does not cause arterial hemorrhage. Observation risks a fatal rebleed.

items.stem: A patient has had a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt placed for recurrent variceal bleeding. Which complication occurs most often in the following months and needs monitoring?
items.explanation: A portosystemic shunt diverts portal blood around the liver, so ammonia and other gut-derived toxins reach the brain, producing new or worsening hepatic encephalopathy in roughly a quarter of patients. It is managed with lactulose and rifaximin and rarely requires shunt reduction. Shunt stenosis is also common but is not the best answer here. Arterial thrombosis, biliary strictures, and portal aneurysm are not typical consequences of this procedure.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman has an incidental 4 cm liver lesion found during evaluation of a kidney stone. She is asymptomatic. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a homogeneous mass with a central stellate scar that enhances late and is isointense on hepatobiliary phase images. Which management is most appropriate?
items.explanation: A central stellate scar and uptake on hepatobiliary-phase imaging characterize focal nodular hyperplasia, a benign hyperplastic response to a vascular malformation. It almost never bleeds or becomes malignant, so an asymptomatic lesion is observed. Resection is reserved for symptoms or diagnostic uncertainty. Ablation and chemoembolization treat tumors that need destruction and expose her to avoidable harm.

items.stem: A 46-year-old man with chronic pancreatitis from hypertriglyceridemia has disabling daily pain despite analgesics and enzyme therapy. Imaging shows a main pancreatic duct dilated to 9 mm with multiple strictures and stones and no head mass. Which operation is best?
options: Total pancreatectomy with islet autotransplant first
items.explanation: A markedly dilated main duct, generally over 7 mm, in chronic pancreatitis with pain is the setting for a lateral drainage operation, longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy, which relieves ductal hypertension and preserves pancreatic tissue. Resection of the head, as in Frey or Beger procedures, is added when an inflammatory head mass exists. Distal resection ignores the ductal disease, and biliary bypass relieves jaundice, not pain.

items.stem: A 49-year-old woman with cirrhosis from primary biliary disease has ascites that returns within one week after each large-volume paracentesis despite maximal diuretics and sodium restriction. Her MELD score is 12, and she has no encephalopathy or heart failure. Which intervention is most appropriate to control the ascites?
items.explanation: Ascites that recurs despite maximal medical therapy is refractory ascites, and a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt reduces portal pressure and controls fluid in selected patients with preserved function and no encephalopathy or heart failure. Peritoneovenous shunts clog and cause coagulopathy. Open surgical shunts carry higher operative mortality. Diaphragmatic fenestration treats a different problem, hepatic hydrothorax from a pleural defect.

items.stem: A 49-year-old woman has recurrent duodenal and jejunal ulcers and chronic diarrhea. Fasting gastrin is greatly elevated, and gastric pH is below 2. Computed tomography shows a 1.5 cm duodenal wall nodule and no liver lesions. After proton pump inhibitor therapy begins, what is the most appropriate next step?
options: Surgical exploration and resection of the tumor with regional lymph node clearance
items.explanation: Recurrent ulcers in unusual locations, diarrhea, and a high gastrin with low gastric pH indicate Zollinger-Ellison syndrome from a gastrinoma, most often in the duodenum or pancreatic head. Acid suppression controls symptoms, and curative resection of the localized tumor with node clearance is advised. Total gastrectomy and vagotomy were historic acid operations that do not treat the tumor, and embolization targets metastatic liver disease.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has a 5 cm liver lesion discovered on ultrasound for gallstones. She has no symptoms and no liver disease. Contrast computed tomography shows peripheral nodular enhancement that fills in centripetally on delayed images. Liver enzymes are normal. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Percutaneous needle biopsy to confirm the diagnosis
items.explanation: Peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal fill-in is the classic pattern of a hepatic hemangioma, the most common benign liver tumor. An asymptomatic lesion needs no treatment regardless of size, and the risk of rupture is very low. Biopsy risks bleeding and adds nothing when imaging is characteristic. Enucleation and embolization are reserved for rare symptomatic or rapidly enlarging lesions.

items.stem: During laparoscopic cholecystectomy the surgeon recognizes that the common hepatic duct has been completely transected and a segment is missing. The patient is stable, and there is no bile peritonitis. Which action is best?
options: Open Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy at an expert center
Primary end-to-end duct repair over a T-tube immediately
Place a drain and finish the operation without repair
Ligate the proximal duct and leave a drain
items.explanation: A transected duct with tissue loss cannot be repaired end to end without tension, which predisposes to stricture. Recognized major injuries are best reconstructed by a Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy, ideally by an experienced hepatobiliary surgeon, with transfer if needed. Leaving the injury or ligating the duct causes biliary fistula, cholangitis, or secondary biliary cirrhosis and a harder later repair.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man has jaundice, and endoscopy shows a 2 cm ulcerated ampullary mass. Biopsy shows adenocarcinoma, and staging shows no vascular invasion or metastases. Which operation is most appropriate?
items.explanation: Invasive ampullary adenocarcinoma is treated with a pancreaticoduodenectomy, which removes the duodenum, ampulla, distal bile duct, and regional nodes, and has better outcomes than pancreatic head cancers. Endoscopic papillectomy is limited to adenomas without invasion. Biliary bypass is palliative, and distal pancreatectomy removes the wrong part of the gland and cannot clear the periampullary nodes.

items.stem: A 22-year-old man is hemodynamically stable after a bicycle fall. Computed tomography shows a grade III splenic laceration with a small hemoperitoneum and no contrast blush. He has no other injuries and a normal abdomen examination. What is the best management?
options: Admission for observation with serial examinations and hemoglobin checks
items.explanation: A stable patient with a moderate splenic injury and no contrast extravasation is managed nonoperatively, in a monitored setting with serial examinations and hemoglobin measurements, because the success rate is high and the spleen's immune function is preserved. Immediate surgery is for instability, peritonitis, or failure of nonoperative care. Discharge is unsafe early because delayed bleeding can occur, and lavage adds nothing after imaging.

items.stem: On day six after a pancreaticoduodenectomy, a patient has fever, mild abdominal pain, and a drain output of 80 mL daily. Drain fluid amylase is 4,800 U/L, compared with a serum level of 90 U/L. He is stable and eating. Which statement best describes the management?
options: Stop the drain to let the fluid reabsorb
Maintain drainage with antibiotics only if infected, as this is a postoperative pancreatic fistula
Start total parenteral nutrition and withhold all oral intake permanently
items.explanation: Drain fluid amylase more than three times the serum level on or after the third postoperative day defines a postoperative pancreatic fistula. Most are managed conservatively with adequate drainage, antibiotics if infection develops, and nutritional support, with reoperation reserved for sepsis or hemorrhage that fails less invasive measures. Removing the drain risks an undrained collection, and universal prolonged fasting is unnecessary in a stable, eating patient.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man with cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis B and ascites is treated with diuretics and large-volume paracentesis. Over three days his creatinine rises from 1.1 to 2.4 mg/dL. Urine sodium is very low, urine sediment is bland, there is no proteinuria, and there is no response to stopping diuretics and a 48-hour albumin challenge. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute tubular necrosis from prolonged ischemia
Hepatorenal syndrome with acute kidney injury
Obstructive uropathy from a ureteral stone
items.explanation: Acute kidney injury in cirrhosis that persists after diuretic withdrawal and albumin expansion, without shock, nephrotoxins, structural kidney disease, bland sediment, and a very low urine sodium, defines hepatorenal syndrome. It reflects splanchnic vasodilation and renal vasoconstriction. Tubular necrosis would show granular casts and higher urine sodium. Obstruction and glomerulonephritis would show hydronephrosis or active sediment and proteinuria.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman at 20 weeks of pregnancy has an incidental 3 cm splenic artery aneurysm on ultrasound. She is asymptomatic. Which statement best guides management?
options: Intervention is advised because rupture risk is high in pregnancy
Observation is safe because aneurysms rupture only after menopause
Rupture risk depends only on calcification, so treatment is never needed
Percutaneous drainage is the preferred treatment
items.explanation: Splenic artery aneurysms in women of childbearing age, especially during pregnancy, carry a risk of rupture with high maternal and fetal mortality, so treatment is advised for lesions of 2 cm or more, or when a woman plans pregnancy. Options include endovascular exclusion or surgical ligation. Calcification does not remove the risk, and drainage is not applicable to a vascular lesion.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has three episodes of acute pancreatitis with no stones, medication cause, or lipid abnormality. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography shows a dorsal duct that drains through the minor papilla and a small ventral duct that does not communicate with it. What is the diagnosis?
options: Sphincter of Oddi dyskinesia of the major papilla
Pancreas divisum with relative obstruction at the minor papilla
items.explanation: Pancreas divisum is failed fusion of the dorsal and ventral ducts, so most pancreatic drainage passes through the small minor papilla. A minority develop recurrent pancreatitis, which may be treated with minor papilla sphincterotomy. Annular pancreas encircles the duodenum and presents with obstruction, and a choledochal cyst involves the bile duct. Sphincter dysfunction affects the major papilla and shows a normal duct anatomy.

items.stem: A 43-year-old woman has right upper quadrant pain after meals for six months. Ultrasound shows multiple gallstones, a normal common bile duct, and a normal wall thickness. She has no fever, and her laboratory values are normal. She wants definitive treatment. Which is the best management?
options: Oral bile acid dissolution therapy as first choice
items.explanation: Symptomatic cholelithiasis with recurrent biliary colic should be treated with elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy, which prevents complications such as cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, and pancreatitis. Dissolution therapy works slowly, only on small cholesterol stones, and stones recur. Sphincterotomy treats bile duct stones, not gallbladder disease. Lithotripsy is rarely used and still leaves behind the gallbladder that forms the stones, so recurrence is expected.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man is admitted with acute pancreatitis from gallstones. Heart rate is 112, and he has received lactated Ringer solution at a moderate rate. Urine output is 0.3 mL per kilogram per hour, hematocrit is rising, and blood urea nitrogen is increasing. Which is the best fluid strategy?
options: Aggressive large-volume boluses regardless of clinical response
Fluid restriction to prevent pulmonary edema
Colloid solution only, to limit tissue edema
items.explanation: Early fluid resuscitation with lactated Ringer solution, targeted to urine output, heart rate, and hemoconcentration and reassessed every few hours, is the cornerstone of care. Excessive fluid increases respiratory complications and abdominal compartment risk without better outcomes, so it is titrated to response. Restriction worsens pancreatic hypoperfusion and necrosis. Colloids offer no advantage over balanced crystalloid.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man has biliary colic with ultrasound showing gallstones and a common bile duct of 8 mm. Bilirubin is 2.8 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase is mildly elevated, and he has no fever or pancreatitis. He is scheduled for cholecystectomy. What is the best next step to evaluate for duct stones?
options: No further evaluation because stones are unlikely
items.explanation: A dilated duct with elevated bilirubin gives an intermediate probability of choledocholithiasis. A noninvasive study, magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography or endoscopic ultrasound, confirms stones before an invasive procedure, or intraoperative cholangiography may be used. Immediate sphincterotomy would expose some patients to unnecessary risk. A nuclear scan evaluates cystic duct patency, not duct stones. Ignoring the findings risks retained stones.

items.stem: A surgical resident is reviewing hepatic segmental anatomy before a right hepatectomy. Which segment is unique because its hepatic veins drain directly into the inferior vena cava, and its portal and arterial supply arises from both the right and left branches?
options: Segment 5, the anterior inferior right segment
Segment 8, the anterior superior right segment
items.explanation: The caudate lobe, segment 1, is supplied by both right and left portal branches and drains by short veins directly into the inferior vena cava, which is why it often hypertrophies in hepatic venous outflow obstruction. Segment 4 drains through the middle hepatic vein and is supplied from the left pedicle. Segments 5 and 8 drain into the right and middle hepatic veins and are supplied by the right anterior sector pedicle.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman presents 30 hours after the onset of constant right upper quadrant pain, fever of 38.4 C, and nausea. Murphy sign is positive. Ultrasound shows gallstones, wall thickening, and pericholecystic fluid. Common bile duct is 4 mm, and liver tests are normal. Which management is best?
options: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy during this admission
Antibiotics alone, with interval cholecystectomy in three months
items.explanation: Acute calculous cholecystitis in a fit patient is best treated with laparoscopic cholecystectomy early in the presentation, ideally within about a week of symptom onset, which shortens stay and avoids recurrent episodes. Delayed surgery risks failure of antibiotics and readmission. With a normal bile duct and liver tests, endoscopic cholangiography is unnecessary. Cholecystostomy is reserved for patients too ill for surgery.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman is recovering after an elective splenectomy for hereditary spherocytosis. Which organisms cause the most severe overwhelming postsplenectomy infection, and which preventive measure is most important?
options: Gram-negative anaerobes, with perioperative antibiotics for six months only
Fungal organisms, with annual antifungal therapy
Encapsulated bacteria such as pneumococcus, with pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Haemophilus vaccination
items.explanation: Without a spleen, clearance of encapsulated organisms, mainly Streptococcus pneumoniae, then Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae, is impaired, and sepsis can progress within hours. Vaccination against all three, patient education about prompt treatment of fever, and in some patients antibiotic prophylaxis form the prevention plan. Anaerobes, viruses, and fungi are not the characteristic pathogens in asplenic patients.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman with colon cancer has three synchronous right-lobe liver metastases. Preoperative volumetry shows that a planned right hepatectomy would leave a future liver remnant of 18 percent of total liver volume, and the liver is otherwise normal. What is the best next step?
options: Proceed with right hepatectomy as planned
Cancel surgery and give only palliative chemotherapy
Portal vein embolization to enlarge the remnant
Perform a left lateral sectionectomy only
items.explanation: A normal liver generally needs a future remnant of at least 20 percent, and more after prolonged chemotherapy or with parenchymal disease. At 18 percent, the risk of postoperative liver failure is high. Portal vein embolization redirects flow to the remnant and induces hypertrophy over several weeks, after which a resection becomes safe. Proceeding invites failure, and a limited operation would leave the tumors behind.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman has an incidental 3 cm pancreatic body cystic lesion. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a cluster of many tiny cysts with a central scar in a honeycomb pattern. She has no symptoms, and the lesion does not communicate with the duct. What is the best management?
options: Observation, with resection reserved for symptoms or growth that causes problems
items.explanation: A honeycomb microcystic lesion with a central scar is a serous cystadenoma, which is almost always benign. An asymptomatic lesion can be observed, and resection is offered for symptoms, uncertain diagnosis, or rapid growth. Distal pancreatectomy and pancreaticoduodenectomy are major operations with real morbidity that are unjustified here, and chemotherapy has no role for a benign cystic neoplasm.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman with severe acute pancreatitis has serum triglycerides of 2,800 mg/dL, normal calcium, a normal gallbladder, and no medication cause. Which therapy addresses the underlying cause most directly during the admission?
items.explanation: Triglycerides above about 1,000 mg/dL can trigger acute pancreatitis. Lowering the level quickly with an insulin infusion, with plasmapheresis for severe or refractory cases, along with fasting and later lipid-lowering therapy, treats the cause. A normal gallbladder makes cholecystectomy pointless. Duct stenting prevents pancreatitis after procedures, and calcium is not indicated because calcium is normal and hypercalcemia, not hypocalcemia, causes pancreatitis.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman with cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis C and tense ascites has fever and abdominal tenderness. Diagnostic paracentesis shows 620 polymorphonuclear cells per cubic millimeter and a culture growing Escherichia coli. Creatinine is 1.4 mg/dL. Which management is most appropriate?
options: Antibiotics alone, without albumin, to avoid volume overload
Large-volume paracentesis with no antibiotic if hemodynamically stable
items.explanation: A polymorphonuclear count above 250 per cubic millimeter in cirrhotic ascites defines spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Treatment is a third-generation cephalosporin plus albumin, which reduces renal failure and mortality, especially with a raised creatinine. Surgery is unnecessary without a perforation source and carries a high mortality in cirrhosis. Omitting antibiotics leaves untreated infection, and omitting albumin forfeits the proven survival benefit.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has a 6 cm multiloculated cystic mass in the pancreatic tail. Fluid has high carcinoembryonic antigen, and the cyst wall contains ovarian-type stroma on cytology. Which management is best?
options: Distal pancreatectomy with splenic preservation if feasible
items.explanation: A solitary mucinous cystic lesion with ovarian-type stroma in a middle-aged woman, usually in the body or tail, is a mucinous cystic neoplasm. These have malignant potential, so resection with a distal pancreatectomy is recommended, preserving the spleen when oncologically safe. Surveillance leaves an at-risk lesion, drainage into the stomach leaves the neoplastic epithelium, and chemotherapy is not a treatment for a resectable benign or in situ cystic neoplasm.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman is admitted with severe acute pancreatitis and persistent respiratory failure and renal insufficiency lasting more than 48 hours. Which term best classifies the severity under the revised Atlanta classification?
options: Mild acute pancreatitis defined by absence of necrosis
Severe acute pancreatitis defined by persistent organ failure
Moderately severe pancreatitis defined by transient organ failure
Severe pancreatitis defined by size of the fluid collection
items.explanation: The revised Atlanta classification grades severity by organ failure and local complications, not imaging collections alone. Mild disease has none, moderately severe disease has local complications or transient organ failure under 48 hours, and severe disease has organ failure persisting beyond 48 hours. Severe disease carries the highest mortality, and the size of a collection does not determine the grade.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man has recurrent mild pancreatitis. Endoscopic ultrasound shows a main pancreatic duct dilated to 8 mm with mucin extruding from a patulous papilla. He is fit for surgery. Which management is most appropriate?
options: Pancreatic resection of the involved segment
Endoscopic stent placement as definitive therapy
items.explanation: Main-duct intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm, with a duct over 5 mm and mucin from the papilla, carries a high risk of high-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma, so resection is recommended in a fit patient. Surveillance suits small branch-duct lesions without worrisome features. Stenting or drainage may relieve obstruction temporarily but leaves the premalignant epithelium. Extent of resection follows the disease distribution.

items.stem: A 57-year-old man has fever, left upper quadrant pain, and left shoulder pain two weeks after endocarditis was treated. Computed tomography shows a single 6 cm peripheral rim-enhancing collection in the spleen. Which management is most appropriate?
options: Antifungal therapy for ten days with no further procedure
Antibiotics and splenectomy or percutaneous drainage depending on the lesion
Splenic artery embolization as the only treatment
items.explanation: A solitary rim-enhancing splenic lesion with sepsis is a splenic abscess, often from hematogenous seeding, as with endocarditis. Treatment is antibiotics with drainage, percutaneous for a single unilocular lesion and splenectomy for multiloculated, multiple, or failed drainage, with vaccination planning. Antibiotics alone are rarely curative in a large abscess, and embolization could worsen infection by causing infarction.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man with compensated cirrhosis from steatotic liver disease has a single 4 cm hepatocellular carcinoma. Child-Pugh class is A with no portal hypertension, and platelets are normal. Which treatment gives the best chance of long-term survival if he is a good operative candidate?
options: Systemic therapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors alone
items.explanation: For a solitary hepatocellular carcinoma in a patient with preserved liver function and no clinically significant portal hypertension, resection offers the best long-term survival. Transplantation is an alternative when function is poor. Systemic therapy is for advanced disease, and whole-liver radiation is poorly tolerated. Embolization is a bridge or palliative option and rarely cures a resectable single tumor.

items.stem: A 57-year-old man has a single 3 cm hepatocellular carcinoma in a cirrhotic liver. He has Child-Pugh class C disease, refractory ascites, and a platelet count of 62,000 per microliter. Resection would be unsafe. Which treatment is the best long-term option?
options: Right hepatectomy with later ablation if recurrence occurs
Palliative care alone because the tumor is malignant
Intravenous chemotherapy with a single cytotoxic agent
Liver transplantation within accepted tumor size criteria
items.explanation: In decompensated cirrhosis with a tumor inside the Milan criteria, a single lesion up to 5 cm or up to three lesions each under 3 cm without vascular invasion, transplantation treats both the cancer and the failing liver and gives the best survival. Resection would risk liver failure. Palliation abandons a curable situation, and cytotoxic chemotherapy has poor activity in this tumor.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man with compensated cirrhosis has a solitary 2.5 cm hepatocellular carcinoma located deep in segment 7 near the diaphragm. His platelets are 58,000 per microliter, he has clinically significant portal hypertension, and he is not a transplant candidate. Which treatment is most appropriate?
items.explanation: For a small solitary hepatocellular carcinoma in a patient with portal hypertension who is not a transplant candidate, local ablation offers survival close to resection with much lower risk of liver failure. Right hepatectomy would likely cause decompensation. Cytotoxic chemotherapy has little benefit, and observation forgoes curative treatment of an early tumor that is amenable to ablation.

items.stem: A 48-year-old man with chronic pancreatitis from hypertriglyceridemia has hematemesis. Endoscopy shows isolated gastric fundal varices without esophageal varices. Liver function is normal, and computed tomography shows a thrombosed splenic vein and a normal portal vein. Which operation addresses the cause?
items.explanation: Isolated gastric varices with a thrombosed splenic vein and normal liver are left-sided, or sinistral, portal hypertension, caused by splenic venous obstruction from pancreatic inflammation. Splenic outflow reroutes through short gastric veins to the stomach. Splenectomy removes the inflow and cures the varices. A transjugular shunt and distal splenorenal shunt treat intrahepatic portal hypertension, and esophageal transection addresses esophageal varices.

items.stem: A 38-year-old farmer from a sheep-raising region has vague right upper quadrant discomfort. Computed tomography shows a 9 cm cystic liver lesion with an internal septated daughter-cyst pattern and a calcified rim. Serology for Echinococcus is positive. Which approach is best?
options: Albendazole and surgery with spillage precautions
Aspiration of the cyst through the skin without any further agent
items.explanation: A septated cyst with daughter cysts and positive serology is a hydatid cyst. Treatment combines albendazole with surgery or carefully performed percutaneous drainage, using a scolicidal agent and avoiding spillage, since leakage can cause anaphylaxis and seeding. Simple aspiration alone risks both. Observation leaves a growing, rupture-prone lesion. Marsupialization into the peritoneum would disseminate the parasite.

items.stem: Pathology after routine laparoscopic cholecystectomy in a 66-year-old woman shows adenocarcinoma invading the muscle layer of the gallbladder wall, with a negative cystic duct margin. Staging imaging shows no distant disease. Which management is most appropriate?
options: Re-resection of segments 4B and 5 with nodes
items.explanation: Incidental invasive gallbladder cancer beyond the mucosa, stage T1b or higher, needs re-resection that includes a wedge of liver around the gallbladder bed, segments 4B and 5, with portal lymph node clearance, once metastatic disease is excluded. Simple cholecystectomy is sufficient only for disease confined to the lamina propria. Observation or radiation alone would leave residual microscopic cancer.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man is brought in after a motor vehicle collision. His blood pressure is 76/40 mm Hg despite resuscitation, with a positive focused assessment of the abdomen for free fluid and left upper quadrant tenderness. Which step is most appropriate?
options: Emergency laparotomy with splenectomy or splenorrhaphy
Computed tomography to grade the injury before any action
Angiographic embolization as the first step
items.explanation: A patient with persistent hypotension and positive free fluid has hemorrhagic shock from intra-abdominal bleeding, and the spleen is the likely source. Emergency laparotomy is mandatory, and splenectomy is usually the safest definitive step in an unstable patient, although repair can be done when the patient is stable. Imaging and angiography delay control of bleeding, and observation is for stable patients only.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman has episodes of confusion and sweating that resolve with eating. During a supervised fast, glucose falls to 38 mg/dL with inappropriately elevated insulin, C-peptide, and proinsulin, and sulfonylurea screening is negative. Computed tomography shows a 1.2 cm enhancing lesion in the pancreatic body, away from the duct. What is the best treatment?
items.explanation: Hypoglycemia relieved by food, with high insulin and C-peptide and negative drug screening, indicates insulinoma, usually a small benign solitary tumor. Enucleation cures most patients when the lesion is superficial and away from the main duct. Pancreaticoduodenectomy and total pancreatectomy are excessive, and diazoxide is only a temporary measure for patients unfit for surgery or with metastatic disease.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man has early satiety and epigastric fullness six weeks after an episode of acute pancreatitis. Computed tomography shows a 9 cm thin-walled peripancreatic collection that compresses the stomach and contains no solid debris. Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: Observation because size alone is an indication to wait
items.explanation: A mature, encapsulated collection without necrotic debris at more than four weeks is a pseudocyst. Intervention is indicated for symptoms such as obstruction, infection, or bleeding, and internal drainage into the stomach, usually endoscopic, is preferred. Observation suits asymptomatic cysts regardless of size. Resection is excessive for a benign collection, and simple aspiration commonly recurs because it does not create a lasting communication.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis C is evaluated for a hernia repair. Which laboratory value contributes to his MELD score but is not part of the Child-Pugh classification?
items.explanation: The MELD score is calculated from serum bilirubin, INR, and creatinine, and current versions add serum sodium. Child-Pugh uses bilirubin, albumin, prothrombin time or INR, ascites, and encephalopathy. Creatinine reflects renal dysfunction and mortality risk, which Child-Pugh omits. Albumin belongs to Child-Pugh but not MELD, while bilirubin and INR appear in both systems, so they cannot distinguish the two.

items.stem: A 46-year-old man returned from rural travel three months ago and now has fever and right upper quadrant pain. Imaging shows a single 8 cm abscess in the right lobe. Aspirate is sterile, brown, and odorless, and serology for Entamoeba histolytica is strongly positive. What is the best treatment?
options: Open surgical drainage with right hepatic lobectomy
Percutaneous drainage plus six weeks of intravenous cephalosporin alone
Metronidazole followed by a luminal agent, with drainage only if complicated
Cholecystectomy with common bile duct exploration
items.explanation: Amebic abscess responds to metronidazole, followed by a luminal amebicide to clear intestinal carriage. Drainage is added only for large left-lobe lesions, impending rupture, or failure to improve in several days. Pyogenic abscesses need drainage and broad antibiotics, but this one has a sterile aspirate and positive serology. Hepatic resection and biliary surgery have no role without a biliary source.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man is two days into mild gallstone pancreatitis. Pain is improving, he is tolerating oral intake, and there is no organ failure or cholangitis. Which timing of cholecystectomy is best?
options: Elective cholecystectomy about six months later
Cholecystectomy only if a second attack occurs
Endoscopic sphincterotomy and no gallbladder surgery in any case
items.explanation: In mild gallstone pancreatitis, cholecystectomy during the same admission, once pain settles, reduces recurrent pancreatitis, readmission, and biliary events. Waiting months leaves a substantial risk of another attack. Sphincterotomy lowers recurrence but is considered mainly when the patient is unfit for surgery. In severe or necrotizing disease, cholecystectomy is delayed until collections resolve or are stable.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman has chronic immune thrombocytopenia with platelet counts of 18,000 per microliter. She has had no sustained response to corticosteroids, immunoglobulin, or second-line medical therapy over 12 months. She has frequent mucosal bleeding. Which management is most appropriate?
options: Splenic artery embolization only as first choice
items.explanation: Splenectomy is considered for chronic immune thrombocytopenia that fails medical treatment, and it induces a durable response in about two thirds of patients. Vaccination against encapsulated organisms is given at least two weeks beforehand when possible. Prolonged steroids carry toxicity, embolization is an alternative only in selected patients, and repeated platelet transfusions are consumed rapidly and may sensitize.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man has fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain. Temperature is 39.2 C, heart rate 118, blood pressure 82/48 mm Hg, and he is confused. Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct with a stone. Bilirubin is 6.4 mg/dL, and white cell count is 21,000 per microliter. Which step is the most important after resuscitation and antibiotics?
options: Repeat imaging in 48 hours to see whether he improves
items.explanation: Fever, jaundice, pain, hypotension, and confusion form Reynolds pentad, indicating severe acute cholangitis. The obstructed infected duct must be decompressed urgently, usually by endoscopic drainage with stone removal or stent placement, with percutaneous drainage as the alternative. Open surgery in an unstable patient carries high mortality. Waiting risks death from sepsis, and oral bile acids do not relieve obstruction.

items.stem: A 71-year-old man has painless jaundice, pruritus, and weight loss. Imaging shows intrahepatic ductal dilation in both lobes, a collapsed gallbladder, a normal common bile duct below the confluence, and a 2 cm mass at the hepatic duct confluence without vascular encasement or distant disease. Which operation offers the only chance of cure?
options: Cholecystectomy with common bile duct excision alone
Internal drainage by choledochojejunostomy to the dilated duct
items.explanation: A mass at the confluence with bilateral ductal dilation and a collapsed gallbladder is a perihilar cholangiocarcinoma. Cure requires an R0 resection, usually a major hepatectomy with caudate lobe removal, since the caudate ducts drain into the confluence, followed by Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy. A Whipple operation addresses distal disease. Simple duct excision leaves tumor, and bypass is palliative.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman who has used oral contraceptives for nine years has sudden right upper quadrant pain and light-headedness. Heart rate is 112 and blood pressure 92/58 mm Hg. Computed tomography shows a 7 cm heterogeneous liver mass with hyperdense fluid around it. Fluid resuscitation stabilizes her. What is the best treatment of the underlying lesion once she is stable?
options: Long-term observation with repeat imaging only
Radiation therapy directed at the mass
Liver transplantation for the benign lesion
items.explanation: A hepatic adenoma larger than 5 cm that has bled carries a risk of rebleeding and malignant transformation, so resection is advised after stabilization, with the hormonal exposure discontinued. Observation is reserved for small lesions that regress after stopping the hormone. Radiation has no role in a benign adenoma. Transplantation is excessive except in rare adenomatosis with unresectable disease or confirmed malignancy.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman underwent splenectomy for immune thrombocytopenia two years ago, with a good initial response. Her platelet count has fallen again to 25,000 per microliter. Blood smear lacks Howell-Jolly bodies. Which finding should be sought?
options: A second malignancy of the liver
An accessory spleen on nuclear imaging or computed tomography
items.explanation: Absence of Howell-Jolly bodies after splenectomy suggests functioning splenic tissue remains, and relapse of thrombocytopenia points to an accessory spleen, found in a minority of people near the splenic hilum, tail of the pancreas, or omentum. Imaging with a nuclear scan or computed tomography localizes it, and resection may restore the response. Liver tumor, biliary obstruction, and portal thrombosis do not explain recurrent immune platelet destruction.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman with long-standing gallstones has jaundice and recurrent right upper quadrant pain. Imaging shows an impacted stone in the gallbladder neck compressing the common hepatic duct, with intrahepatic ductal dilation above the compression. What is this condition called?
items.explanation: Mirizzi syndrome results from extrinsic compression of the common hepatic duct by a stone impacted in the cystic duct or gallbladder neck, sometimes with a cholecystocholedochal fistula. Bouveret syndrome is a stone passing through a fistula to cause gastric outlet obstruction, and gallstone ileus produces small bowel obstruction. Caroli disease is a congenital segmental dilation of intrahepatic bile ducts, unrelated to impacted stones.
